newsitem.title: USA: US Treasury bond retreats from key 6.50-pct level.
newsitem.headline: US Treasury bond retreats from key 6.50-pct level.

text.p: The 30-year Treasury bond gave up some ground as its momentous three-week rally showed signs of running out of steam at the key 6.50-percent barrier, traders said.

Other Treasury maturities slipped in sympathy in a lethargic market following the extended President's Day weekend. Retail was on the sidelines and dealers found no trading incentive in a thin calendar of U.S. economic data.
"The market needs fresh news to trade on. It would take something new to take us through 6.50 percent," a trader said.
The 6.50-percent February 2027 30-year Treasury bond shed 8/32 to 101 to yield 6.55 percent vs 6.53 percent on Friday.
Friday's yield was the lowest since a recent high of 6.94 percent set on January 27 amid fears the fourth-quarter Employment Cost Index would deliver bad wage inflation news.
But since, reassuring wage and inflation data as well as the Federal Reserve's decision to keep interest rates unchanged fueled the rally that peaked on Friday.
"We've been in that range around 6.75 percent for a while. To really break below 6.50 percent or above 7.0 percent would take something else," the bond trader added.

The most noticeable news of the day -- a 2.8-percent rise in the Lynch, Jones and Ryan Inc Redbook retail sales index for the first two weeks of February versus January -- did not provide any trading opportunity.
It just confirmed the American consumer remains as eager to spend as he was during the 1996 Christmas shopping spree.
The trader also doubted that the Consumer Price Index for January would prove much of a market-mover when it is released Wednesday at 0830 EST/1230 GMT.
"The market expects CPI up 0.3 percent, the core a bit less. Nothing that would really change the picture," he added.
The consensus in a Reuters survey expects the January CPI up 0.3 percent, and ex-food, ex-energy core CPI up 0.2 percent.

Goldman, Sachs and Co. economist John Youngdahl agrees the market needs a major new development to pack fresh momentum and break through the 6.50-percent level -- and if not, more range-trading as seen on Tuesday is in the cards.

"We have been of the view for some time that, somewhere around 6.50 percent, this rally would run out of steam," Youngdahl said. "It's difficult to pinpoint at what yield exactly, but it's around 6.50 percent."

The Goldman, Sachs economist pointed out the "market has essentially taken out most -- if not all -- of the tightening risks, and the short-term rate structure has squeezed out tightening prospects betweeen now and the summer."

Eurodollar contracts, federal funds rate futures, and the six-month Treasury bill -- down one point to a 5.03-percent rate and 5.23-percent yield -- showed the market has not priced in any rate hike by the Fed on the near-term horizon.
"To make a sustained move through the current levels, you would have to see some information that would allow the market to conclude an easing is reasonable," Youngdahl added.
Amid the lack of prospects for a fresh Treasuries rally, investors continued to pump funds into U.S. equities as the Dow Jones index closed at yet another record.
"Stocks, here or in Europe, are a tough competition for Treasuries right now," a dealer at a European firm noted.
The three-month Treasury bill rate was unchanged at 4.99 percent, and the one-year rate up one point at 5.16 percent.
The two-year note was down 1/32 at 100-5/32 and 5.79 percent, the five-year down 1/32 at 100-24/32 and 6.07 percent, and the 10-year off 3/32 at 99-25/32 and 6.28 percent. (( -- 212-859-1666 ))
